newsitem.title: UK: British newspapers tip Blair as new prime minister.
newsitem.headline: British newspapers tip Blair as new prime minister.

text.p: Most British newspapers were convinced on Thursday Tony Blair would lead his Labour Party to a general election victory that would return it to power after 18 years in opposition.
"Blair heading for Number 10 (the prime minister's residence), say the (opinion) polls" was the headline in the Times.
The right-wing Daily Telegraph, a traditional supporter of the ruling Conservative Party, splashed Prime Minister John Major's last-ditch appeal "Don't give up on us" as its headline.
But another headline in the newspaper said: "Tory (Conservative) support is lowest ever for an eve of election poll."
For Blair, who at 43 would become Britain's youngest prime minister if he was elected on Thursday, the most cherished front-page picture could be the one in the tabloid Sun.
This showed a sparkling finger pointing to Blair's smiling face with the caption "It must be you" in a take-off of adverts for Britain's national lottery.
In 1992, the Sun claimed it had secured Labour's general election defeat through its vicious campaign against Blair's predecessor Neil Kinnock.
But on Thursday, the Sun told voters: "Today you have a unique opportunity to join the greatest jackpot syndicate ever...all you have to do is vote Labour."

With opinion polls showing that up to half of Britain's 44 million voters have yet to decide who to vote for, nearly all the papers made a point of urging readers to make the effort to go to polling stations.
"Your vote is vital," said the headline over the Daily Telegraph's editorial.
The left-wing Daily Mirror tabloid devoted several pages to urging readers to "Get Even Today" after 18 years of Conservative rule.

The right-wing Daily Mail maintained its support for the Conservatives. "If the don't-knows and undecideds swing behind John Major in the privacy of the voting booth, they could yet trigger an unprecedented fifth Tory term of office," the paper said. Several columnists wrote farewell messages to Major.

"History will not be kind to John Major," said Polly Toynbee in the Independent. "Our children in 50 years' time will scratch their heads and try to remember who came in the fallow years between (Margaret) Thatcher and Blair."
Conservative member of parliament turned columnist Matthew Parris wrote a fonder tribute from the last day on Major's campaign trail.
"That this press conference could change nothing rendered all the more noteworthy the poise, civility and good grace with which the prime minister conducted it," Parris said.

The Conservatives, however, had not given up the fight. They took out a full page advert in some papers picturing a smiling Major and asking voters, "Why Risk a Change?...Don't Let Labour Ruin It Again."
